title: Thermodynamics
tagline: Heat, work, entropy and the ideal gas
summary: Temperature and the equation of state, the first and second laws, heat engines, entropy, thermodynamic potentials, and the kinetic theory of gases.
overview: Thermodynamics describes matter in bulk without committing itself to what the matter is made of. Energy can enter as heat or as work, and not every form of energy is equally available for work: that restriction is the second law, and entropy is the quantity that expresses it. The subject is short on new equations and strict about what they mean.

We begin with temperature, heat capacity and the ideal gas, then the first law and the kinds of process — isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric, isochoric — that make up an engine. Kinetic theory supplies a microscopic reading of pressure and temperature for a dilute gas, before the second law, entropy and the potentials U, H, F and G. The potentials are the language of the later course on statistical mechanics.

Signs are a frequent source of trouble. This course takes work done on the system as positive in the first law, ΔU = Q + W, and says so whenever the opposite convention would change a formula. Quasi-static is not the same as reversible, and an ideal gas is a model with PV = nRT and U depending only on T, not a description of every gas.
outcomes: Use the ideal-gas law, heat capacities and the difference Cp − Cv = nR.
Apply the first law to isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes.
Derive the pressure of an ideal gas from molecular collisions, and use the Maxwell speed distribution at the level of its consequences.
Compute the efficiency of a Carnot engine and state why no engine between the same two temperatures can do better.
Calculate entropy changes for reversible processes and for the free expansion of an ideal gas.
Use the thermodynamic identity dU = T dS − P dV and the potentials H, F and G, including Maxwell relations in simple cases.

history.title: Boyle’s law
history.detail: The second edition of Boyle’s New Experiments recorded that, at fixed temperature, the pressure of a confined sample of air is inversely proportional to its volume.

history.title: Carnot’s engine
history.detail: Sadi Carnot’s Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire showed that the efficiency of a reversible engine depends only on the two temperatures it works between.

history.title: The first and second laws
history.detail: Clausius and, independently, William Thomson (Kelvin) stated energy conservation for heat and work, and the principle that heat does not pass of itself from a colder body to a hotter one.

history.title: Kinetic theory
history.detail: Clausius, and then Maxwell in 1860, derived the pressure of a gas from molecular impacts and found the distribution of molecular speeds.

history.title: Entropy named
history.detail: Clausius introduced entropy and summarised the two laws as: the energy of the universe is constant, and its entropy tends to a maximum.

history.title: Boltzmann’s principle
history.detail: Boltzmann related the entropy of a macrostate to the number of microstates, S = k log W, the bridge from this course to statistical mechanics.
